brief.notification_title: Oil near $117 Brent; Fed and Big Tech week ahead
brief.market_summary: US stocks ended the week lower on Friday. The S&P 500 fell 0.52% to 7,623.68 and the Dow lost 1.23% (−653 pts) as AXP slid. Front-month Brent settled at $116.72 (+3.1%), its highest settlement since April, after reports that the US and Israel may strike Iran again. Treasuries sold off modestly: the 10Y rose 3.5bp to 4.988% but is still 11bp lower on the week. Crypto stayed soft over the weekend, with BTC at $80.7k and ETH at $2,377 (−11.5% over the month) as spot ETF outflows continued. The coming week brings the FOMC on Wednesday, Microsoft and Alphabet that evening, Q3 GDP, September PCE and Amazon on Thursday, and OPEC+ on 1 Nov.
brief.since_last: This is the first brief, so there is no prior to compare against. The news window covers only one hour of Saturday morning with two headlines, and only n2 (BTC near $80k, ETH near $2,370 on weak institutional flows) is relevant. Everything else comes from Friday's close. One data quirk: the 03:17 Singapore timestamp maps to Friday afternoon in New York, but the closing reports (6:35 PM ET) and the snapshot both show the week as finished, so I treat Friday's closes as final. US cash markets reopen Monday 09:30 ET. Oil and crypto will trade any weekend Iran headlines first.

economic_data.takeaway: This is a 53-month high, new orders grew at the fastest pace in more than 4.5 years, and selling prices rose at the sharpest rate since Aug 2022. Strong demand plus rising prices gives the Fed no reason to cut and keeps the inflation side of the oil shock alive.
Services were in line and cooled slightly from a very high level. Growth is still strong and there is no sign of a slowdown.
In line. The economy is running hot, which supports a Fed hold, not cuts.

The final reading beat the preliminary, but the level is very depressed. Current conditions fell to 46.7 from 50.9, while expectations rose to 48.8. Households feel squeezed by energy prices even though business surveys are strong, which is a mildly stagflationary mix.
In line but rising. Combined with $100+ oil, this is the expectations drift the Fed cannot ignore. It supports the 91% priced odds of a hold and caps how far front-end yields can fall.
My sources didn't have the actual figure. Housing is a secondary input this week.
A strong print would confirm the PMI's manufacturing strength and add modest upward pressure on yields before the Fed.

economic_data.expected: Hold at 3.75–4.00% (91% priced; 94 of 100 economists in a Reuters poll)
economic_data.takeaway: The hold is priced, so the guidance is what moves markets. A hawkish tone about oil passing into prices would hit duration and long-duration tech. Note that the 13-week bill at 4.03% already sits above the 4.00% top of the range, so markets price no cuts.

economic_data.release: Q3 GDP (advance) and Sep PCE / core PCE
economic_data.takeaway: These land the day after the Fed, so the Fed decides without the PCE print. A hot core PCE could undo a dovish-sounding press conference within 18 hours. This is the key data risk for bonds this week.

earnings.takeaway: The stock fell 3.7%, the worst in the Dow, and was the main reason the Dow fell 1.23%. An EPS beat built on cost cuts while revenue missed got sold, which shows how high the bar is for consumer-finance names. XLF fell 1.32%.

earnings.takeaway: Shares rose about 4.6%. An oil-services beat with stronger guidance is the first earnings evidence that $100+ crude is reaching energy profits. It supports XLE (+2.6% Friday).

earnings.takeaway: The stock gained about 4% after hours, then reversed to about −6.5% on input costs and higher capex. This is a classic beat-and-fade in AI hardware. It sets a cautious tone for STX (Tue) and SNDK (Thu).

earnings.takeaway: The stock fell about 11% despite a large beat and a raise. When crowded AI-power names sell off on good news, positioning is stretched, not fundamentals.

earnings.result: Missed: HOKA and UGG revenue came in below FactSet estimates. I couldn't verify the exact EPS and revenue.
earnings.takeaway: Down 6.7% pre-market. Together with the weak UMich current-conditions reading, this suggests discretionary demand is softening.

It reports four hours after the Fed. Azure growth and capex guidance will drive SMH, which is −12.2% over the month, and the Nasdaq. After WDC and BE, expect a beat to be necessary but possibly not sufficient.
Together with MSFT, this is a combined ~$7.8T of index weight reporting on Fed night. It is the biggest single equity event of the quarter.
It lands the same day as GDP and PCE. AWS and the consumer read-through matter after the AXP and DECK signals.
This is the first big test of refiners' windfall margins. SHEL ($3.25 est) and TTE ($3.99 est) report Thursday pre-market. Strong numbers would back the XLE idea.
Telecoms fell Friday (VZ −3.6%, T −4.2%, TMUS −4.3% pre-market) on a Bloomberg report that SpaceX is in talks to lease 80,000 cell towers. Listen on the call for comments on competition and pricing.

earnings.takeaway: Intel has been rising (+1.7% Friday on an FCC waiver). The conflicting estimates make the bar unclear, so be careful reading headline beat/miss claims.

sections.summary: Indices fell modestly Friday on oil-driven inflation worries before the Fed. The index level hides a sharp rotation: semis are down 12% over the month while energy, staples and utilities are up 8–11%. Beat-and-fade reactions (WDC, BE, AXP) show that good news is not enough heading into the busiest earnings week of the season.
key_points: 1-month sector moves: SMH −12.2%, XLK −5.9% vs XLE +10.75%, XLU +8.1%, XLP +8.0%, XLV +5.5%. Friday partly reversed this: XLK +0.49%, SMH +0.74%, XLP −1.92%.
VIX 19.45 (+24% m). CFTC speculators are net short 142.7K S&P contracts (prior 141.0K) and net long 50.7K Nasdaq 100.
Telecoms fell on the SpaceX tower-leasing report while tower owners rose (CCI +7.6%, AMT +5.5%). Apple hit a record high on iPhone Duo sell-outs.

sections.summary: Yields rose 3–4bp Friday after a hot manufacturing PMI and rising inflation expectations, but the 10Y and 30Y are still 11–12bp lower on the week. Bills at 4.03% sit above the 4.00% top of the Fed range, so markets price no cuts. The week brings ~$180B of 2/5/7Y supply, a Fed hold, and PCE the day after.
key_points: Inflation inputs are rising: PMI selling prices rose at the sharpest rate since Aug 2022, UMich 1Y expectations are 4.7% and 5Y 3.5% (both up 0.1pt), and Brent is around $117.
Auctions: 2Y Mon (~$69B), 5Y Tue (~$70B), 2Y FRN Wed, 7Y Thu (~$44B). Sizes are unconfirmed.
Credit: LQD −0.41% d; HYG −1.08% m, a mild weakening in high yield.

sections.summary: Front-month Brent settled at $116.72 (+3.1%), its highest settlement since April, on reports of possible US/Israeli strikes on Iran and attacks on Saudi infrastructure. Physical supply is genuinely short: Gulf exports run at 60–80% of normal and US inventories drew more than expected. The weekly picture is a war premium on top of a real deficit, which means big two-way headline risk.
key_points: Data caution: the snapshot shows BZ=F at $111.70 (−1.30%), which conflicts with the reported $116.72 settle and BNO's +3.02%. The snapshot is most likely quoting a later contract month near the Dec expiry, which would imply a steep ~$5 backwardation. I use $116.72 as the front month.
WTI settled at $103.27 (+3.8%). A ~$13 Brent–WTI spread signals that the shortage is in seaborne, Middle East barrels.

Supply hits: Houthi strikes, with Aramco evacuating staff from its Dhahran headquarters; the Libyan Zawya pipeline shut; a second US carrier heading to the region. ING calls its $80 Q4 forecast 'unattainable'.

EIA crude draw of 3.06M bbl vs −0.1M expected; the SPR is reportedly at its lowest since 1982. The US oil rig count is 460 (+1), so there is no supply response yet. CFTC crude net long fell to 89.3K from 100.3K, so speculators are not chasing. OPEC+ meets 1 Nov.

sections.summary: BTC is holding near $80.7k, but the complex is bleeding on persistent spot ETF outflows. ETH and the alt L1s are clearly underperforming. Tech's sell-off spilled into crypto Friday and there is no flow catalyst in sight before the Fed.
key_points: Spot BTC ETFs saw −$635.6M on 22 Oct and roughly −$138M on 23 Oct (preliminary). Spot ETH ETFs saw −$110.6M and −$46.5M; October ETH ETF outflows total $1.08B, the largest month of 2026.
Ethereum's Glamsterdam testnet upgrade was reportedly delayed over EIP-8037 griefing risk. This comes from a search summary and is unconfirmed.
On regulation: a senator's inquiry to Tether, and South Korea moving to treat stablecoins as payment instruments under its forex law. No SEC action.

brief.instructor_take: Next week packs most of the quarter's event risk into four days: the Fed Wednesday at 2pm, Microsoft and Alphabet that evening, GDP, PCE and Amazon Thursday, the BoJ Friday and OPEC+ on Sunday. My view is that the real driver is not the Fed hold, which is 91% priced, but the oil shock passing into prices. The PMI shows selling prices rising at the fastest rate since 2022, consumers' inflation expectations are creeping up, and bills already yield above the top of the Fed range, so cuts aren't coming. What a less experienced investor may miss is the order of events: the Fed decides without September PCE, so a calm press conference on Wednesday can be overturned by a hot core PCE on Thursday morning. In equities, the S&P is down only 1% on the month, but underneath semis are down 12% and energy and defensives up 8–11%. That is a rotation toward real-asset cash flows, not a crash, and the beat-and-fade reactions at WDC and Bloom tell me AI hardware is still too crowded to buy on good news. So I'd go into the week with dry powder in T-bills, own the oil shock through producers whose earnings are already showing it rather than chasing $117 futures, and stay out of the weakest corner of crypto until ETF outflows stop. Two things would prove me wrong: a credible US–Iran de-escalation, which would deflate oil and the energy trade fast, or blowout Azure and Google Cloud numbers with steady capex, which would spark a sharp tech rebound and make cash look timid. I'm candid that the oil call depends on headlines, which is why it's the smaller position.

top_ideas.title: Park dry powder in T-bills through Fed week
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills pay ~4% while the Fed, PCE and Big Tech land in 48 hours
top_ideas.thesis: The 13-week bill yields 4.03%, above the top of the 3.75–4.00% Fed range, so cash earns a real return with almost no price risk. With the Fed, MSFT and GOOGL, GDP, PCE and AMZN clustered Wednesday to Thursday, holding cash means I can buy any dislocation instead of being forced into one. BIL is an equivalent alternative.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start from the yield curve. Bills at 4.03% tell me the market prices no cuts, so short paper doesn't lose income to a cut any time soon. Next I look at the event calendar, and I see unusual clustering: the Fed decides Wednesday without the PCE print that arrives Thursday morning, and roughly $10T of mega-cap stocks report around those two days. The concept is optionality. Cash in bills is a free option to buy after the uncertainty clears, and its price barely moves either way. I prefer SGOV to IEF or TLT because the inflation inputs (PMI prices at a 2022-era pace, Brent at $117, rising UMich expectations) argue against taking duration risk into a possibly hot PCE and ~$180B of auctions. What a less experienced investor may miss is that 'doing nothing' at 4% is a position with a better risk/reward than most trades this week. I'd change my mind if the Fed signalled cuts, in which case I'd extend into IEF, or if the 10Y broke clearly above 5.15% after PCE, which would make locking in duration attractive.
catalysts: Thu 29 Oct Q3 GDP and Sep PCE 08:30 ET
risks: Opportunity cost if MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN spark a broad rally
A surprise dovish Fed pivot would lower bill yields over time (limited near-term impact)
top_ideas.entry: Buy Monday at the open with cash earmarked for new positions. No timing needed.
top_ideas.invalidation: A Fed statement opening the door to near-term cuts (rotate part of it into IEF), or a 10Y yield above 5.15% after PCE, which would make extending duration the better use.
top_ideas.sizing: Hold the cash reserve here, e.g. 10–20% of the portfolio, to be redeployed after 29 Oct

top_ideas.title: Own the oil shock via producers, not futures
top_ideas.one_liner: Energy earnings are catching up to $117 Brent; scale in, don't chase
top_ideas.thesis: Brent's front month settled at $116.72 on a real supply deficit (Gulf exports at 60–80% of normal, a 3.06M bbl US draw, the SPR at a 1982 low), and SLB's beat-and-raise shows it is reaching profits. XLE is up 10.75% on the month, much less than the crude move, and pays out cash flow rather than depending on futures rolls. BNO is the purer Brent alternative but carries more headline risk.
top_ideas.reasoning: The evidence chain runs from physical shortage to price to earnings. Inventories drew 3.06M bbl against −0.1M expected, Gulf exports are impaired, Libya lost a pipeline and US rigs aren't responding (460, +1). SLB then beat ($0.64 vs $0.61–0.62) and guided Q4 revenue to ~$10B, which is the first proof that this reaches income statements, and PSX (est $12.02 vs $2.52), SHEL and TTE report next week. I prefer XLE to BNO because producers are pricing a lower long-run oil price than spot, which gives a cushion if the war premium fades, while BNO would take the full hit from a ceasefire headline. One useful tell: CFTC speculators cut their crude net long to 89.3K from 100.3K even as prices rose, so this rally isn't a crowded speculative trade. What a less experienced investor may miss is that geopolitical premiums can vanish overnight, so I scale in rather than buying after a +2.6% day. I'd be wrong if a credible US–Iran de-escalation sent Brent back under $100, or if refiner and major earnings show costs eating the windfall.
catalysts: Wed 28 Oct PSX earnings and EIA inventories
Thu 29 Oct SHEL and TTE earnings
risks: US–Iran de-escalation collapsing the war premium
Demand destruction or a growth scare if the Fed turns hawkish
A coordinated stock release (the SPR is already depleted, which limits this)
top_ideas.entry: Buy half Monday near $69, the remaining half on a pullback toward $67 or after PSX/SHEL/TTE confirm, spread over the week.
top_ideas.invalidation: XLE closing below $65.50, or front-month Brent settling below $100 on de-escalation news.
top_ideas.sizing: 2–3% of the portfolio in total, built in two tranches

top_ideas.title: Stay out of ETH and alt L1s until flows turn
top_ideas.one_liner: Record ETH ETF outflows; ETH down 11% in a month as BTC holds $80k
top_ideas.thesis: ETH is down 11.5% on the month against BTC's −3.9%, with October ETH ETF outflows of $1.08B, the worst month of 2026, and outflows on each of the last two days. Alt L1s (SOL, XRP, ADA, AVAX, TON) are down 11–14%. Until institutional flows stop leaving, the weakest asset in a weak complex is a falling knife.
top_ideas.reasoning: I'm applying relative strength: in a drawdown, capital leaves the weakest assets first and returns to the strongest. BTC is near $80.7k and only modestly lower, while ETH, SOL and XRP have lost three times as much, so the market is clearly choosing BTC and BNB over the rest. The flow data explains why: spot ETH ETFs bled −$110.6M and −$46.5M on the last two days for $1.08B in October, and n2 cites weak institutional flows. There is also a possible fundamental negative in the reported Glamsterdam testnet delay, though I treat that as unconfirmed. A cheaper price is not by itself a reason to buy. A less experienced investor sees '−11% means a bargain' when what matters is whether sellers are done, and ETF flow is the cleanest gauge of that. Crypto also trades weekends and Fed Wednesday, so a hawkish surprise would hit it with no circuit breaker. I'd change my view if ETH reclaimed about $2,700 (roughly its level a month ago) alongside several straight days of ETF inflows. If you need crypto exposure, a small spot BTC ETF position after the Fed is the better vehicle.
catalysts: Daily spot ETH/BTC ETF flow prints
Weekend price action around Iran headlines
risks: A short squeeze or sharp rebound if the Fed is less hawkish than feared
ETF flows reversing quickly, leaving you out of a bounce
top_ideas.entry: No new buying. If you already hold ETH or alt L1s, don't average down; consider trimming any bounces toward $2,500.
top_ideas.invalidation: ETH reclaiming $2,700 with three or more consecutive days of net spot ETH ETF inflows.
top_ideas.sizing: 0% new allocation; keep any existing ETH and alt L1 holdings at or below current weight

lesson.explanation: When oil is scarce now, near-month futures trade above later months, a curve shape called backwardation. Funds that hold futures, like BNO, sell the expiring contract and buy a cheaper later one, which earns a positive 'roll yield' while the curve stays that way. The steep curve also tells you the market sees the shortage as temporary: it is paying up for barrels today but expects lower prices later. That is why energy stocks, valued on long-run prices, have risen less than spot crude.
lesson.todays_example: Brent's front month settled at $116.72 while the snapshot shows $111.70 for what is most likely a later contract, a gap of roughly $5. BNO is up 14.8% over the month and XLE 10.75%: producers are priced off the lower future price, not the $117 spot.
